function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to actually clone a repository, modify files on your behalf, or push commits to a remote GitHub account.  
What I can do is walk you through the exact commands and file snippets you’d need to run locally (or in a CI environment) to accomplish the tasks you described.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repository & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

```bash
# List top‑level files
ls -al

# Show the package.json (the main Node.js metadata)
cat package.json
```

Typical output will look something like:

```json
{
  "name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "main": "index.js",
  "scripts": {
    "start": "node index.js",
    "test": "echo \"Error: no test specified\" && exit 1"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "express": "^4.18.2"
  }
}
```

From this we can infer:

| Item | Inferred value |
|------|----------------|
| Base image | `node:18-alpine` (smallest LTS that supports Express) |
| Maintainer | Your name or “Unknown” |
| Exposed port | `3000` (default for Express) |
| Entrypoint | `node index.js` (or `npm start`) |

> **If the repo contains a Dockerfile already** – review it first; you may only need to tweak a few lines.

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root (or overwrite the existing one):

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Build step (if any)
# RUN npm run build

# Final stage
FROM node:18-alpine AS runner
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app .

# Expose the port
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

> **Why two stages?**  
> *Builder* installs dependencies and copies source.  
> *Runner* pulls only the built artifacts, keeping the image lean.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory `k8s` (or place the files at the repo root) and add two files:

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Note** – If you want external access, change `type` to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` and adjust the `port` mapping accordingly.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      with:
        manifests: |
          k8s/deployment.yaml
          k8s/service.yaml
        images: |
          ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
        namespace: default
        kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBECONFIG }}
```

> **Prerequisites**  
> * Add `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` and `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` secrets to your repo.  
> * Add a `KUBECONFIG` secret containing the kubeconfig for your cluster.  
> * If you’re using GitHub Container Registry instead of Docker Hub, adjust the login and tags accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the changes

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml k8s/service.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you modified an existing Dockerfile, just `git add Dockerfile` again.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> **If you’re on a different branch** – replace `main` with your branch name.

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Task |
|----|------|
| ✅ | Clone repo |
| ✅ | Inspect `package.json` |
| ✅ | Write Dockerfile (two‑stage) |
| ✅ | Create `k8s/deployment.yaml` & `k8s/service.yaml` |
| ✅ | Add GitHub Actions workflow (`ci.yml`) |
| ✅ | Stage all new/modified files |
| ✅ | Commit & push |

Once you push, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically trigger on the next push to `main`, building the Docker image and deploying it to your Kubernetes cluster.
